title: I Was Wrong About Mini-Whiteboards
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A teacher writing as SoL in the Wild confesses that, until recently, mini-whiteboards meant only review games like trashketball, and describes how a Steplab Great Teaching Unpacked episode changed that view. Seeing whiteboards used at critical points to check what secondary students actually knew, the author recasts them as a tool for assessment for, not of, learning that opens the black box of student thinking. The argument is anchored in Ausubel's claim, cited through Kirschner and Hendrick's How Learning Happens, that the most important single factor influencing learning is what the learner already knows. From that principle the author concludes that a teacher needs a fast way to ascertain what every student knows and adapt accordingly, and that mini-whiteboards fit because any question, prompt or task can be assigned, shown and adapted. The post ends with seven concrete strategies, including activating prior knowledge, dual-coded sketches, retrieval practice, re-engaging attention with quick this-or-that questions, modelling exemplar responses, and mini-debates. It is a short, reflective, practical piece rather than a research review.
points: The author's turn is from treating mini-whiteboards as a game prop to using them as a whole-class window into student thinking at critical points in a lesson.
Ausubel's dictum that what the learner already knows is the most important single factor supplies the theoretical case for constantly checking prior knowledge and teaching adaptively.
The versatility argument is that any question, prompt or task can be assigned, shown and adapted, which makes whiteboards more flexible than most assessment routines.

Seven strategies span activating prior knowledge, dual coding, retrieval practice, regaining attention, modelling exemplars and structured mini-debates, so one cheap tool serves several evidence-informed moves.
The honest framing, I was wrong, shows a teacher revising a long-held view after seeing a model of practice, rather than adopting a fashionable technique.
quotes: After viewing Episode 1 of Steplab’s Great Teaching Unpacked, there was a paradigm shift in my perspective of what and how mini-whiteboards could be leveraged as an “assessment for, not of learning” tool. I saw the simplest of technologies being used in the most powerful ways.

The boards became a window into the “black box” of student thinking, knowledge, and understanding. A way to assess what was going right, going wrong, and teach adaptively based on the data in the “black box”.
Not an important factor. The most important single factor. My job as an educator is to influence learning.
But how can I quickly and effectively “ascertain” what every single student in my classroom knows at any given time? And adapt my teaching based on what students know or do not know?

It became apparent that mini-whiteboards are not only extremely simple to use but there is nothing you cannot do with them. They are versatile in a way that many other assessment strategies are not. Any question.

I realized this is how I should have been teaching all along. In a way that influences learning by determining what students know and teaching based on the “most important single factor influencing learning.
